citeAs: Li, Y., Du, Y., Zhou, K., Wang, J., Zhao, W. X., & Wen, J.-R. (2023). Evaluating Object Hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models. arXiv preprint arXiv:2305.10355v3.
creator: Yifan Li, Yifan Du, Kun Zhou, Jinpeng Wang, Wayne Xin Zhao, Ji-Rong Wen (Renmin University of China, Meituan Group)
description: POPE (Polling-based Object Probing Evaluation) is a dataset and evaluation method designed to assess object hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs). It formulates evaluation as a binary classification task by prompting LVLMs with simple Yes-or-No questions about probing objects in an image.
name: POPE
publisher: Renmin University of China, Meituan Group
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: POPE formulates the evaluation of object hallucination as a binary classification task. Questions whose answers are 'Yes' are built using ground-truth objects, while questions with the answer 'No' are built by sampling from negative objects. The ratio between ground-truth and nonexistent objects is set as 1:1 for label balance.
rai:dataBiases: The paper notes that LVLMs are prone to hallucinate frequently appearing objects in the visual instruction datasets, as well as objects that frequently co-occur with ground-truth objects in the image. POPE includes Popular and Adversarial sampling strategies to specifically probe these biases.
rai:dataCollection: POPE constructs a set of triples consisting of an image, multiple questions, and their answers ('Yes' or 'No'). Objects are obtained either from existing human annotations or automatic segmentation tools like SEEM. Negative objects are sampled using three strategies: Random Sampling, Popular Sampling, and Adversarial Sampling.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Images and annotations from existing datasets including MSCOCO, A-OKVQA, and GQA.
rai:dataLimitations: The dataset only focuses on object hallucination and does not measure overall LVLM capacity. The matching-based method to determine 'Yes' or 'No' answers may fail if LVLMs do not explicitly output these words. When using automatic segmentation tools, the annotated objects depend on the tool's label set, which may diverge from human annotations.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Negative objects are sampled using three strategies: Random Sampling (random nonexistent objects), Popular Sampling (top-k most frequent objects in the dataset that do not exist in the image), and Adversarial Sampling (top-k frequent objects that co-occur with ground-truth objects but do not exist in the image).
rai:dataSocialImpact: The paper notes that object hallucination hinders the safe use of LVLMs in real-world deployment, potentially leading to unexpected consequences such as autonomous driving systems making wrong decisions due to incorrect understanding of the external environment.
rai:dataUseCases: Evaluating object hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs).
rai:machineAnnotationTools: Automatic segmentation tools like SEEM (Segment Everything Everywhere All at Once) are used to extract objects from unannotated images.
